title: Effects of sound masking noise on workers' perception and performance
research_question: How does sound masking noise affect employee perception and psychological endurance in demanding jobs in the open plan office, specifically considering both good signal speech noise and bad signal speech noise?

participants.description: 7 participants (4 male, 3 female) aged between 25 and 39, recruited from Concordia University, Montreal, Quebec, Canada. Excluded 3 participants due to inability to complete tasks or abnormal responses. All had normal hearing and vision.
participants.recruitment: Participants scheduled appointments via Calendly, compensated with a $30 Amazon gift card for a two-hour VR experience over four sessions.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 3D virtual open-plan office environment (68.5 sq meters, 2.7m height) designed in Unity, including computer screen, 5 tables, 21 chairs, 4 windows, 3 diffusers, 3 doors. Visuals rendered for Oculus Quest 2.

Four noise conditions: 1. Pink noise at 38 dBA. 2. Pink noise at 50 dBA. 3. Pink noise at 38 dBA with speech signal at 53 dBA (SNR 15). 4. Pink noise at 50 dBA with speech signal at 53 dBA (SNR 3). Speech content from UW/NU Corpus (Harvard IEEE sentences) by 20 distinct speakers. Each condition played for 40 minutes.

measures.instrument: Number of math tasks completed (out of 3 for Task 1, out of 108 for Task 2)
Percentage of correct answers in math tasks

findings.antecedent: 50 dBA pink noise with 53 dBA speech

findings.mechanism: Accuracy fluctuates significantly with the level and type of noise, highlighting sensitivity to noise.

findings.antecedent: 38 dBA pink noise with 53 dBA speech
findings.mechanism: Speech, even at low background noise levels, can raise cognitive demands.

At a higher noise level of 50 dBA without speech, the average cognitive load was 10.59, and the standard deviation was 3.81.

findings.antecedent: 50 dBA pink noise with 53 dBA speech

findings.mechanism: Speech, due to its rich information nature, may require additional cognitive resources for processing or ignoring, exacerbating noise impact.
findings.quote: increasing environmental noise is associated with negative impacts on cognitive perception and task performance.

mechanisms: Speech, due to its rich information nature, may require additional cognitive resources for processing or ignoring, thereby exacerbating the impact of noise on human cognitive performance.
The combination of higher noise levels and speech (bad signal-to-noise ratio for speech) significantly hampers task efficiency.
Speech in high background noise conditions may have a focusing effect or provide a cognitive support to enhance task accuracy.
Individual differences in noise sensitivity lead to varied experiences of task load and performance outcomes.
The presence of speech introduces additional cognitive processing demands, dispersing attention and increasing cognitive load.
Increased noise levels cause attention and cognitive abilities to be more dispersed, further increasing cognitive load.

Continuous background noise from sound masking systems may exacerbate sensitivity to sound changes, heightening discomfort and reducing working ability, especially for those accustomed to irregular noise.
Irregular noise can easily trigger a stress response, especially when perceived as a threatening sound.
implementation_implications: Designers for architecture and acoustic design should consider noise sensitivity as an important factor in sound design of workplaces, especially for tasks requiring high concentration.
Before implementing noise control measures in open-plan offices, the specific characteristics of environmental issues and personal sensitivities of employees must be assessed.
When employees find sound masking annoying, other adaptive noise control technologies that adjust masking levels based on changing noise environments may be more appropriate.

limitations: Small sample size (N=7) from a convenience sample at Concordia University, limiting generalizability.
Reliance on self-report measures for noise perception, which may introduce biases and not capture the full range of participants' experiences.
Virtual reality systems primarily focus on visual and auditory perception, with limited simulation of other senses (e.g., touch, skin sensations), potentially leading to human perception bias.
Differences between VR headset images (resolution, color reproduction) and the real world may impact sound perception and not fully replicate real-life office conditions.
The weight of the Oculus Quest 2 (503g) may cause head fatigue and a sense of heaviness during longer sessions, potentially restricting head movements.
Cultural and individual differences among participants may affect the accuracy and reliability of data and responses to experimental tasks or sound.
